title: Sensory and Motor Neurons
intro: At one end of the nervous system, receptor cells and the circuits right behind them turn light, sound, touch and chemicals into spike trains. At the other, motor neurons turn spike trains into muscle force. Both ends have been modelled for decades with unusual accuracy, because their inputs or outputs can be controlled and measured exactly, and both are directly useful to an SNN builder: one tells you what realistic input spike trains look like, the other how a spiking output drives the body.

items: Graded before spiking: photoreceptors, hair cells and retinal bipolar cells do not spike; they signal with graded potentials and continuous transmitter release. Spikes start only at the first neuron whose axon must travel far (retinal ganglion cells, auditory nerve fibres).
Adaptation everywhere: receptors and early neurons adapt to the mean level of their input on several timescales, so they report changes and contrast rather than absolute values.
ON and OFF channels: many sensory systems split signals into cells that respond to increases and cells that respond to decreases, the origin of event-camera-like coding.
Recruitment at the output: motor neurons are recruited in order of size, so force is controlled by how many and which units are active, as well as by their rates.
Retinal Neurons (#/neuroscience/cell-types/sensory-and-motor/retinal): photoreceptors, bipolar, horizontal, amacrine and ganglion cells, and the LN and GLM models that predict ganglion cell spikes.

Cochlear Hair Cells (#/neuroscience/cell-types/sensory-and-motor/hair-cell): inner and outer hair cells, ribbon synapses and phase locking, and the Meddis and Zilany-Bruce-Carney models that generate auditory nerve spike trains.
Touch Receptors (#/neuroscience/cell-types/sensory-and-motor/touch-receptor): the four classes of mechanoreceptive afferent in the hand, first-spike coding, and the TouchSim model.
Spinal Motor Neurons (#/neuroscience/cell-types/sensory-and-motor/motor-neuron): the size principle, persistent inward currents and plateau potentials, and the Booth-Rinzel-Kiehn model.

Olfactory receptor neurons: each expresses one receptor type, about 50 in fly and about 400 in human; same-type axons converge onto glomeruli (see Mushroom Bodies, #/neuroscience/mushroom-bodies, for what happens next in insects).

blocks.text: Sources: Henneman, E. (1957). Relation between size of neurons and their susceptibility to discharge. Science; Masland, R. H. (2012). The neuronal organization of the retina. Neuron.
